---
title: "How long one worldwide day takes to process"
subtitle: "Where the time went on 14 June 2026, what was changed, and what is left"
author: "EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit"
date: last-modified
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(knitr)

# Read-only. Every number and table on this page comes from a CSV file in
# data/, written by benchmarks/day_timing.py and benchmarks/day_compare.py of
# the opdi repository. Nothing here reads S3, a database or a Spark cluster:
# data/_manifest.json records, for each file, the script, the git commit and a
# fingerprint of the source files.
D <- function(f) read.csv(file.path("data", f), stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                          colClasses = c(step = "character"))

ds <- D("day_summary.csv")      # one row per step: before and after, how obtained
st <- D("step_timings.csv")     # one row per run of a step (label = which run)
sg <- D("stage_timings.csv")    # one row per Spark stage of each run of a step
rc <- read.csv(file.path("data", "result_comparison.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

num <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")

# One value of day_summary.csv, of step_timings.csv, and the executor-seconds
# (sum of the run time of all tasks) of one run of one step.
S  <- function(step, col) ds[ds$step == step, col]
ST <- function(label, step, col = "seconds") st[st$label == label & st$step == step, col]
ES <- function(label, step) sum(sg$executor_run_s[sg$label == label & sg$step == step])

before_total <- S("total", "before_s")
after_total  <- S("total", "after_s")

# The share of the cores at work, from the scaling rule written in the notes
# of the "total" row ("... / (16 cores x 0.85) ...").
busy <- as.numeric(sub(".*x ([0-9.]+)\\).*", "\\1", S("total", "notes")))

# Scale factors: the 4-hour slice by rows (from step_timings.csv), the
# aircraft sample by its modulus ("hash(icao24) % 12 == 0").
sf_slice <- as.numeric(ST("scaled_new", "01", "scale_factor"))
sample_m <- as.numeric(sub(".*% ([0-9]+) ==.*", "\\1", ST("m12new", "02", "scope")))

# Executor-seconds of a full day with the new code, step by step.
work <- c(
  "01"  = ES("s4new", "01") * sf_slice,
  "02"  = ES("m12new", "02") * sample_m,
  "02a" = ES("m12new", "02a") * sample_m,
  "03"  = ES("v2", "03"),
  "04"  = ES("v2", "04"),
  "04b" = ES("v2", "04b"),
  "09"  = ES("v2", "09")
)
cores_now <- as.numeric(ST("v2", "03", "executors")) * as.numeric(ST("v2", "03", "cores"))
cores_old <- as.numeric(ST("base", "03", "executors")) * as.numeric(ST("base", "03", "cores"))
work_total <- sum(work)

# Result comparison.
R <- function(part, item, col) rc[rc$part == part & rc$item == item, col]
ev <- rc[rc$part == "events", ]
info_n <- as.numeric(sub(" matched events differ", "", R("event field", "info", "note")))
info_types <- ev$item[grepl("info differs", ev$note)]

# The ingestion time of the ADS-C study, for the caution at the end.
pt <- read.csv(file.path("..", "adsc-effect-v1", "data", "processing_time.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(step = "character"))
ar <- read.csv(file.path("..", "adsc-effect-v1", "data", "adsc_reports.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

## Summary

Processing one worldwide day of OpenSky data, 14 June 2026, took about
`r num(before_total)` s (`r num(before_total / 3600, 1)` hours) before this
work and about `r num(after_total)` s (`r num(after_total / 3600, 1)` hours)
after it. The gain came from five changes to the code, which removed repeated
or badly spread work, and from running 12 Spark executors instead of 8. The
published results did not change, and the target of one hour per day was not
reached: the work that remains needs more processors than the cluster has, or
a different way of building tracks.

## What was measured

The pipeline turns OpenSky position reports into tracks, a flight list and
flight events in a chain of numbered steps (see
[Processing steps](../../content/methods/pipeline.qmd)). It runs on Apache
Spark, which splits each step into **stages** and each stage into **tasks**
that run in parallel. A task runs on an **executor**, a worker process with 2
processor cores and 14 GiB of memory.

The day measured is 14 June 2026, worldwide: `r num(R("flight list", "flights", "after"))`
flights and `r num(R("file flight_events", "rows", "after"))` events. The same
day was run before and after the changes on the OpenSky cluster. "Before" is
the code as it was, with `r ST("base", "03", "executors")` executors
(`r cores_old` cores). "After" is the changed code with
`r ST("v2", "03", "executors")` executors (`r cores_now` cores), the most the
cluster's allowance holds: 30 processors and 192 GiB of memory, of which the
process that directs the work takes 4 processors and 16 GiB.

### Four steps measured, three scaled

Steps 03, 04, 04b and 09 were measured on the full day. Steps 01, 02 and 02a
were not: their full-day output did not fit in the storage available. They were run on part of the day and scaled up:

- Step 01 (read and thin the reports) ran on the first 2 and the first 4
  hours of the day.
- Steps 02 (build the tracks) and 02a (clean them) ran on all the hours that
  step 02 reads, but only for one aircraft in `r sample_m` (and, as a check,
  one in 24), chosen by a hash of the aircraft address.

A small part of a day runs in one or two rounds of tasks, so its own run time
says little about a full day. The scaling therefore uses the
**executor-seconds** of the part: the sum of the run times of all its tasks.
The rule is

> full-day time = executor-seconds of the part × scale factor ÷ (cores × `r busy`)
> \+ time of the stages that run as a single task × scale factor

The scale factor is the share of the day the part stands for:
`r num(sf_slice, 2)` for the 4-hour slice (the day has
`r num(sf_slice, 2)` times as many reports) and `r sample_m` for one aircraft
in `r sample_m`. The cores are those of the run (`r cores_old` before); on
average `r num(100 * busy)`% of them were at work in the full-day steps. For
example, the 4-hour slice of step 01 used `r num(ES("s4base", "01"))`
executor-seconds before the changes, which gives
`r num(ES("s4base", "01"))` × `r num(sf_slice, 2)` ÷ (`r cores_old` × `r busy`) =
`r num(S("01", "before_s"))` s. Steps 01 to 02a were timed with
`r ST("base", "03", "executors")` executors in both versions; the "after"
figure assumes that 12 executors do the same work 1.5 times as fast.

## Time per step

```{r tbl-steps}
#| echo: false
names_ <- c("01" = "read and thin the reports", "02" = "build the tracks",
            "02a" = "clean the tracks", "03" = "flight list",
            "04" = "events and measurements", "04b" = "milestones into the flight list",
            "09" = "published files", "total" = "all steps")
how <- ifelse(grepl("full day", ds$after_scope), "measured on the full day",
       ifelse(grepl("4 h", ds$after_scope), "scaled from a 4-hour slice",
       ifelse(grepl("aircraft", ds$after_scope), paste("scaled from one aircraft in", sample_m),
              ds$after_scope)))
tab <- data.frame(step = ds$step, what = names_[ds$step],
                  before = num(ds$before_s), after = num(ds$after_s), how = how)
kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrl",
      col.names = c("Step", "What it does", "Before (s)", "After (s)", "How the figure was obtained"),
      caption = paste0("Time of each step for 14 June 2026, worldwide. Before: ",
                       ST("base", "03", "executors"), " executors; after: ",
                       ST("v2", "03", "executors"), " executors."))
```

```{r fig-steps}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Time of each step before and after the changes, in seconds. Steps 01, 02 and 02a are scaled from part of the day; the others are measured on the full day."
#| fig-height: 4
x <- ds[ds$step != "total", ]
m <- rbind(before = x$before_s, after = x$after_s)
colnames(m) <- x$step
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
barplot(m, beside = TRUE, col = c("grey70", "steelblue"), border = NA,
        xlab = "Step", ylab = "Time (s)", las = 1,
        legend.text = c("before", "after"),
        args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n"))
```

Steps 04 and 02 took most of the time before, and still do.

## What was slow, and what was changed

The Spark log of each run gives one row per stage, with its run time, number
of tasks and longest task. Reading these rows step by step showed five
causes.

1. **Holding patterns were computed twice.** The start and the end of a
   holding pattern were produced by two branches of one query, and Spark
   computed the whole holding calculation once for each branch. Both events
   are now read from one computation.
2. **A look-ahead to the end of each track was repeated for every report.**
   The holding and FIR-crossing steps asked, for each report, a question
   about all the later reports of its track. Spark re-reads that whole range
   for every report, so the cost grows with the square of the track length.
   The same question is now asked by reading the track backwards, where the
   range grows by one report at a time.
3. **Whole-day tables were written by a single task.** The tracks, the events
   and the measurements of a day were each sent to one task before writing,
   so one task did the work of the whole day. They are now spread over many
   tasks.
4. **A reference table was stored as thousands of small files.** The table of
   airport zones (the map cells around each airport) was 7,783 small files,
   and the flight-list step read it three times, opening every file each
   time. It is now 8 files, read once per step and kept in memory.
5. **The raw archive was read three times.** Step 01 counted the rows, then
   listed the days, then wrote them: three reads of the archive. It now reads
   it once.

Two smaller changes go with these: step 02 now leaves out, before building
tracks, the aircraft that have no report on the day (they cannot have a track
that starts on it), and the flight-list step sends the two end reports of each
track to the airport zones instead of moving both tables.

Finally, the number of executors went from 8 to 12. @tbl-runs separates the
two effects for the steps measured on the full day: the middle column is the
new code with the old number of executors.

```{r tbl-runs}
#| echo: false
steps <- c("03", "04", "04b", "09")
r <- data.frame(
  step = steps,
  base = num(sapply(steps, function(s) ST("base", s))),
  v1 = num(sapply(steps, function(s) ST("v1", s))),
  v2 = num(sapply(steps, function(s) ST("v2", s))),
  es_base = num(sapply(steps, function(s) ES("base", s))),
  es_v2 = num(sapply(steps, function(s) ES("v2", s)))
)
kable(r, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr",
      col.names = c("Step",
                    paste0("Old code, ", ST("base", "03", "executors"), " executors (s)"),
                    paste0("New code, ", ST("v1", "03", "executors"), " executors (s)"),
                    paste0("New code, ", ST("v2", "03", "executors"), " executors (s)"),
                    "Executor-seconds, old code", "Executor-seconds, new code"),
      caption = "The steps measured on the full day, in three runs.")
```

With the same 8 executors, the new code took step 04 from
`r num(ST("base", "04"))` s to `r num(ST("v1", "04"))` s and step 03 from
`r num(ST("base", "03"))` s to `r num(ST("v1", "03"))` s; the 12 executors
then brought them to `r num(ST("v2", "04"))` s and `r num(ST("v2", "03"))` s.
Step 09 took longer in the middle run (`r num(ST("v1", "09"))` s); this was not
looked into, and it took `r num(ST("v2", "09"))` s in the last run. For the
scaled steps, the 4-hour slice of step 01 fell from
`r num(ES("s4base", "01"))` to `r num(ES("s4new", "01"))` executor-seconds,
and step 02 on one aircraft in `r sample_m` from `r num(ST("m12base", "02"))` s
to `r num(ST("m12new", "02"))` s. Step 02a was not changed; its gain is the
number of executors.

## The results did not change

The outputs of the day before and after the changes were matched flight by
flight and event by event.

```{r tbl-results}
#| echo: false
fl <- rc[rc$part == "flight list" & rc$item == "flights", ]
ms <- rc[rc$part == "measurement", ]
evf <- rc[rc$part == "event field", ]
res <- data.frame(
  what = c("Flights in the flight list",
           "Flights with a different departure or destination airport",
           "Events (all types)",
           "Events matched on flight, type and time",
           "Matched events with a measurement differing by more than 0.000001",
           "Matched events with a different position or altitude",
           "Matched events with a different info text"),
  value = c(num(fl$after),
            num(sum(as.numeric(regmatches(fl$note, gregexpr("[0-9]+", fl$note))[[1]]))),
            num(sum(ev$after)),
            num(sum(ev$matched)),
            num(sum(as.numeric(sub(" matched.*", "", ms$note)))),
            num(sum(as.numeric(sub(" matched.*", "", evf$note[evf$item != "info"])))),
            num(info_n))
)
kable(res, row.names = FALSE, align = "lr", col.names = c("", "After the changes"),
      caption = paste0("The day after the changes compared with the day before. Before: ",
                       num(fl$before), " flights and ", num(sum(ev$before)), " events."))
```

Every flight has the same departure and destination airports, every event is
found again with the same flight, type and time, and every measurement is
equal. The one difference is the `info` text of
`r num(info_n)` events (`r num(100 * info_n / R("event field", "info", "matched"), 1)`%),
all of them airport-surface events and block times
(`r paste0("\x60", info_types, "\x60", collapse = ", ")`). Their `info` names the
taxiway, apron or stand the aircraft is on. Where one map cell lies on two such
parts of the airport, the event names one of them, and which one depends on
the order in which Spark happens to process the rows. That choice also changes
between two runs of unchanged code, so it is not caused by the changes.

## Why one hour was not reached

Adding up the executor-seconds of each step gives the work a day needs with
the new code:

```{r tbl-work}
#| echo: false
w <- data.frame(step = names(work), es = num(work),
                share = paste0(num(100 * work / work_total), "%"))
w <- rbind(w, data.frame(step = "all", es = num(work_total), share = "100%"))
kable(w, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr",
      col.names = c("Step", "Executor-seconds", "Share"),
      caption = paste0("Work of one worldwide day with the new code. Steps 01 to 02a are scaled as ",
                       "described above, the others measured."))
```

That is about `r num(round(work_total, -3))` executor-seconds. With
`r cores_now` cores at work `r num(100 * busy)`% of the time, it takes about
`r num(work_total / (cores_now * busy))` s, well over the 3,600 s of one hour.
The largest part is step 02, which builds the tracks
(`r num(100 * work[["02"]] / work_total)`%; with the cleaning of step 02a,
`r num(100 * (work[["02"]] + work[["02a"]]) / work_total)`%). To give each
day's tracks their full length, step 02 reads 59 hours of reports for each
day, so every report is split into tracks on two or three different days.

So a day in one hour needs one of two things:

- **More cores.** The work alone asks for about
  `r num(work_total / (3600 * busy))` cores busy `r num(100 * busy)`% of the
  time, against `r cores_now` today; the stages that run as a single task do
  not get faster with more cores, so in practice about twice today's number.
- **A track step that works incrementally**: tracks built once per hour of
  reports, with the tracks still open carried from one day to the next. This
  would remove most of the repeated reading in step 02.

## Limits

- One day was measured. A busier day takes longer.
- Steps 01, 02 and 02a are scaled, not measured, and they are about
  `r num(100 * (S("01", "after_s") + S("02", "after_s") + S("02a", "after_s")) / after_total)`%
  of the time after the changes. They should be timed again on a full day
  when there is enough storage.
- The scaled figure for step 01 may be too low. In a separate study, reading
  `r num(3 * 24)` hours of the archive for only the
  `r num(ar$value[ar$metric == "study_aircraft"])` aircraft that sent ADS-C
  reports that day took `r num(pt$shared_inputs[pt$step == "01"])` s on 12
  executors ([ADS-C study](../adsc-effect-v1/index.qmd)). That run is not a
  daily step 01, which reads one day for all aircraft, but it suggests that
  reading the archive costs more than the 4-hour slice shows.
- The "after" figures of the scaled steps assume that 12 executors are 1.5
  times as fast as 8. For step 02 on one aircraft in 24, 12 executors took
  `r num(ST("m24e12", "02"))` s against `r num(ST("m24new", "02"))` s with 8:
  on a part that small, more executors do not help, which is why the scaling
  goes by cores and not by measured time.

## Provenance

Every number and table on this page is read from the CSV files in `data/` when
the page is rendered; nothing is computed on a cluster, and the page needs no
credentials. The files were written by `benchmarks/day_timing.py` (times per
step and per Spark stage) and `benchmarks/day_compare.py` (comparison of the
outputs) of the opdi repository. `data/_manifest.json` records, for each file,
the script, the git commit, whether the working copy had uncommitted changes
and a fingerprint of the source files. In `step_timings.csv` the run labels
are: `base` the old code, `v1` the new code with 8 executors, `v2` the new
code with 12 executors; `s2`/`s4` are the 2- and 4-hour slices and `m12`/`m24`
the aircraft samples (`base` and `new` for old and new code). The caution on
step 01 reads `papers/adsc-effect-v1/data/processing_time.csv`.
